title: What is recursion — a function that calls itself; it needs a base case (when to stop) and a recursive case (when to call itself again).

s1_definition.profdef: Recursion is a technique where a method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every correct recursive method has two parts: a base case that returns a direct answer without recursing and stops the chain, and a recursive case that reduces the problem and calls the method again. Each call gets its own stack frame on the call stack, and the frames unwind as the base case is reached.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh wants to know the total balance across a chain of linked savings accounts, where each account points to the next one. Instead of writing one giant loop, he asks a simple question: "What is my balance plus the total of the rest of the chain?" To find "the total of the rest", he asks the exact same question about the next account. This keeps going until he reaches the last account that points to nothing — that is the stopping point. Then the answers add back up the chain.
s1_definition.oneliner: Recursion is a method solving a big problem by calling itself on a smaller problem until a base case stops it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Recursion is a technique where a method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every correct recursive method has two parts: a base case that returns a direct answer without recursing and stops the chain, and a recursive case that reduces the problem and calls the method again. Each call gets its own stack frame on the call stack, and the frames unwind as the base case is reached.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh wants to know the total balance across a chain of linked savings accounts, where each account points to the next one. Instead of writing one giant loop, he asks a simple question: "What is my balance plus the total of the rest of the chain?" To find "the total of the rest", he asks the exact same question about the next account. This keeps going until he reaches the last account that points to nothing — that is the stopping point. Then the answers add back up the chain.

**One line to remember:** Recursion is a method solving a big problem by calling itself on a smaller problem until a base case stops it.

sections.s2_technical:
A recursive method must shrink the problem on every call, otherwise it will call itself forever and the call stack overflows. This is why the base case is not optional — it is the safety brake that guarantees the recursion ends.

The base case is the simplest input where you already know the answer directly. For example, in summing a chain of account balances, the base case is an empty chain whose total is zero: `if (account == null) return BigDecimal.ZERO;`. The recursive case does a little work and then delegates the rest to itself with a smaller input, like `return account.getBalance().add(sumChain(account.getNext()));` which adds this account's balance to the total of the remaining chain.

Every recursive call pushes a new frame onto the call stack. That frame stores the local variables and the point to return to. When the base case returns, the frames pop off one by one and combine their results on the way back up. This is why deep recursion can throw a `StackOverflowError` — each frame uses memory, and there is a limit.

A senior-level nuance is tail recursion. If the recursive call is the very last thing the method does, some languages optimise it into a loop so the stack does not grow. The JVM does not perform this optimisation automatically, so for very deep problems in Java we often convert recursion to an explicit loop or an explicit stack to avoid the overflow. Recursion is most valuable when the problem is naturally self-similar, such as traversing trees, walking linked structures, or dividing and conquering sorted data.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a customer can set up a chain of sweep accounts where any surplus in one account flows to the next linked account. Rajesh wants the combined balance of his entire sweep chain. The chain can be any length, so we cannot hardcode how many accounts to add. This is a naturally self-similar problem — the total of the whole chain is this account's balance plus the total of the smaller chain that follows. That is exactly recursion.

Problem 2 — The chain must stop somewhere. The last account in the chain points to nothing. When we reach that point there is nothing more to add, so we return zero. That is the base case that stops the recursion safely.

In our mini-project we build a `SweepAccount` node that holds a balance and a reference to the next account, and a `SweepCalculator` with a recursive `totalBalance` method. The demo links three of Rajesh's sweep accounts and computes the combined balance, logging each recursive step.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a sweep chain SWP-1 (100000) to SWP-2 (50000) to SWP-3 (25000) to null.

Step 1: We call `totalBalance(SWP-1)`. SWP-1 is not null, so this is the recursive case. It needs the total of the rest, so it calls `totalBalance(SWP-2)` and waits.

Step 2: Inside `totalBalance(SWP-2)`, SWP-2 is not null, so it calls `totalBalance(SWP-3)` and waits. Two frames are now paused on the stack.

Step 3: Inside `totalBalance(SWP-3)`, SWP-3 is not null, so it calls `totalBalance(null)` and waits. Three frames are now paused.

Step 4: `totalBalance(null)` hits the base case and returns zero immediately. This is the deepest point of the recursion.

Step 5: Control returns to SWP-3's frame. It computes 25000 plus 0 equals 25000 and returns that.

Step 6: Control returns to SWP-2's frame. It computes 50000 plus 25000 equals 75000 and returns that.

Step 7: Control returns to SWP-1's frame. It computes 100000 plus 75000 equals 175000 and returns the final answer.

```
[2026-10-26 19:30:05] INFO    Visiting SWP-1 balance Rs.100000
[2026-10-26 19:30:05] INFO    Visiting SWP-2 balance Rs.50000
[2026-10-26 19:30:05] INFO    Visiting SWP-3 balance Rs.25000
[2026-10-26 19:30:05] INFO    Combined sweep balance for Rajesh: Rs.175000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  totalBalance(SWP-1 = 100000)
    │ needs rest → calls down
    ▼
  totalBalance(SWP-2 = 50000)
    │ needs rest → calls down
    ▼
  totalBalance(SWP-3 = 25000)
    │ needs rest → calls down
    ▼
  totalBalance(null) ──► BASE CASE returns 0
    ▲
    │ unwind and add back up
  SWP-3: 25000 + 0      = 25000
  SWP-2: 50000 + 25000  = 75000
  SWP-1: 100000 + 75000 = 175000  ◄── final answer
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Recursion is a technique where a method solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every correct recursive method has two essential parts. The base case is the simplest input where the answer is known directly, and it stops the recursion. The recursive case does a small piece of work and then calls the method again on a reduced input. Without a proper base case the method would call itself forever and the call stack would overflow.

The way I explain it from real experience is through my sweep account feature at the National Bank of India. A customer can link savings accounts into a chain where surplus flows from one account to the next. To compute the combined balance of the whole chain I ask a simple self-similar question: the total is this account's balance plus the total of the rest of the chain. To find the total of the rest, I ask the exact same question about the next account, and so on, until I reach the end of the chain where there is nothing left to add and I return zero.

What makes this work correctly is the call stack. Each recursive call gets its own frame that remembers where to return. As I go deeper the frames pile up, and when the base case returns, the frames unwind one by one and the balances add back up from the bottom. So the deepest call returns first and the original call returns last with the final total.

The senior-level point I always add is about limits. Java does not optimise tail recursion automatically, so very deep recursion can throw a StackOverflowError. For problems that could go thousands of levels deep, I convert the recursion into an explicit loop or an explicit stack. Recursion shines when the structure is naturally self-similar, like walking linked account chains, traversing trees, or dividing sorted data, which is why I reach for it in exactly those situations and prefer iteration elsewhere.

keyPoints: Recursion: base case + recursive case — solve smaller subproblem
